title: Planted by streams (Psalm 1)
hookLine: the one who delights in Torah is like a tree planted by streams of water

lines: THE BOOK OPENS WITH A TREE.
cards: Somewhere near where you live there's probably an old tree that has stood through heat waves and storms and whole seasons of your life. What keeps it standing? Not how tall it looks.
What you can't see: the roots, and the water they've found. The Book of Psalms could have opened with thunder or kings or battles. Its very first psalm opens with a person, and then a tree.

teach.b: Psalm one begins with the word ashrei: happy, or fortunate.
Happy is the one who doesn't walk in the counsel of the wicked, or stand in the way of sinners, or sit in the seat of the scornful. Notice the slide: walking, standing, sitting.
It's how people drift: passing by, then lingering, then settling in. Instead, this person's delight is in the Torah of the Lord, and they meditate on it day and night.
Then the picture: "And he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, that bringeth forth its fruit in its season, and whose leaf doth not wither." Look at the details.
Planted, not wild: someone set it there on purpose, near the water. Streams, plural: channels of water running to it. Fruit in its season: not every day, not on demand, but when the time is right.
And the leaf doesn't wither, even in dry weather. Then the contrast.
The wicked are like chaff, the husks the wind blows off the threshing floor. Light, rootless, gone.

The psalm isn't promising that good people never suffer; the Psalms are too honest for that. It's describing roots. A person who keeps going back to the water, day and night, grows something that holds.
And that closes a week: a song without words, raising the sparks, the Maggid's circle, opponents and neighbors, the story that healed, the Psalms, and today, the tree by the stream.

how: Psalm 1 opens the Book of Psalms, so it comes first whenever someone recites Tehillim from the beginning; its tree is often used in Jewish teaching about Torah study.

o: righteous, the one who keeps every law
happy, or fortunate; the first word of Psalm 1
a royal title, like Your Majesty

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.

s: the Book of Psalms opens with a battle
it opens with a person and a tree planted by streams.
the tree bears fruit in its season, not all the time
fruit comes when the time is right.
Psalm 1 promises good people will never suffer
it describes roots that hold, not a life without trouble.

games.q: a hot, dry summer comes. two trees stand in the same field. one's leaves wither, one's don't. what's the difference?
o: the green one is planted by streams of water.
games.why: Psalm 1: the one planted by streams of water, whose leaf does not wither. what holds is the roots and the water they've found.

practice: Sit where you can see a tree or a plant, or run a little water in a glass and watch it, or just picture one, and think about its roots.
Then ask: where are my streams, the text, person, practice or place I keep going back to that keeps me green? Let one come to mind, and if you pray, give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Ashrei, Hebrew for happy, or fortunate, the word that opens Psalm one. Its picture of a person rooted in Torah: a tree by the water, fruit in its season, a leaf that doesn't wither.

orig.note: Hebrew: streams of water, channels, from Psalm 1:3.

carryVoice: Your line: planted by the streams. The leaf doesn't wither. Day three hundred fifteen closes the week.
